source: JMIR Biomedical Engineering (2026) validation of NDM-inspired prompts (recognition-primed, data-frame) for care-seeking advice
finding: Search snippet only (page would not load). Prompts built from Klein's recognition-primed decision model and data-frame theory raised LLM triage accuracy over a default prompt.
numbers: Overall accuracy: default 63.3%, recognition-primed 67.6%, data-frame 66.7%. Self-care class: 13.4% default to 29.8% recognition-primed. Model names and N not read.
limits: Not opened. Numbers come from a search summary and must be re-checked in the paper. Single domain (care-seeking).
agent_relevance: The only direct test found of a macrocognition method as a prompt. Gain is a few points overall but large on the rare, hard class. Worth copying as an operator test; verify first.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5 case study
finding: GPT-3.5 shows anchoring like humans. Low-anchor mean estimate 20.83 (CI 13.92-27.74), high-anchor 105.97 (CI 87.40-124.54). Humans (N=60): 22.5 and 80.50.
numbers: Anchor effect: ChatGPT t(58)=8.78, p<.0001; humans t(58)=5.55, p<.0001. Five ChatGPT-4 trials per anchor: means 22.0 and 94.33.
limits: One model family, small trial counts per cell, 2023 model. Resemblance of output does not show the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: A model fed a number in context is pulled toward it. Any scaffold that shows a first estimate to later steps imports anchoring. Show candidates without prior numbers.

source: Suri et al. (2023) GPT-3.5 heuristics, conjunction and framing studies
finding: ChatGPT chose the conjunction (Linda bank teller and feminist) 18 of 20 times. Framing: all 11 positive-frame trials rated medicine efficacy 5, all 11 negative-frame trials rated 4 (1-7 scale).
numbers: Humans: positive frame 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37), negative 4.6 (CI 4.35-4.85), t(80)=3.86, p<.001; 44 positive and 39 negative participants.
limits: Zero variance in the model across trials means the effect is deterministic and prompt-bound. Only GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Framing of the same facts flips ratings with no variance. Restating a problem in a neutral form (a restate operator) can cut this, but needs testing on our model.

source: Suri et al. (2023) GPT-3.5 heuristics, endowment effect
finding: ChatGPT kept the owned coin in 92.5% of trials (CI 79.6-98.4). 34 of 40 humans (85%, CI 70.1-94.3) did the same.
limits: Role-play framing needed in some prompts; the model sometimes protested it could not imagine owning a coin.
agent_relevance: Human-like bias strength in a model is not evidence the model reasons like a human. Do not treat model output as a stand-in for expert intuition.

source: Horowitz and Plonsky (2025) LLM agents display human biases but exhibit distinct learning patterns
finding: In repeated choice with feedback (GPT-4o mini, Gemini-1.5 Flash), models underweight rare events like humans but follow recent outcomes far more.
numbers: Match to a pure Recency Player: models 78-91% of decisions, humans 67%. Rare-event task 1, B choice: humans 71%, models 74-90%. 160 agents per task vs 110 Prolific humans.
limits: Two proprietary models, four tasks, human samples at least 25 per task, some LLM analyses not shown. Prompt variants (persona) untested.
agent_relevance: Models adapt like a recency heuristic, not like an expert building a situation model. Long-horizon sensemaking needs external state kept by code.

source: Horowitz and Plonsky (2025) surprise and wavy recency
finding: Humans switch more after a surprising outcome (surprise triggers change). Models show no such effect, and their reaction to a rare event dies out by lag 2; humans show a wavy delayed pattern.
numbers: Humans task 1: switch away from B 33% after -10 vs 22% after +1. Task 2: switch to B 31% after +10 vs 15% after -1.
limits: LLM surprise analyses reported as not shown. Provides no scaffold result.
agent_relevance: Models lack a built-in expectancy-violation trigger. Macrocognition says surprise should start re-framing. Our impasse detector in code supplies what the model lacks (supports G1).

source: Horowitz and Plonsky (2025) context manipulation
finding: Giving the full history in every prompt versus chat memory changed behavior little and inconsistently. Temperature 0.2, 1, 2 had little effect.
numbers: Rare-event task 2 B rate: GPT-all 33%, GPT-chat 49%; Gemini-all 16%, Gemini-chat 14%; humans 28%.
limits: Effects small and not consistent across models.
agent_relevance: Simply adding more history is not a fix. Structured summaries from code are a better test than raw logs.

source: Nguyen, Jamale, Gonzalez (2024) Predicting human action decisions: LLMs and cognitive instance-based learning
finding: Llama-3 70B and Mistral 7B predicted human gridworld paths about as well as an ACT-R instance-based learning model; IBL won early, LLMs won over full episodes.
numbers: Accuracy Exp1 simple: Llama 0.651, Mistral 0.658, IBL 0.688. Exp2 complex: 0.542, 0.602, 0.382. 400 human MTurk participants, 40 episodes each.
limits: Open models only, no fine-tuning, simple tasks, loss aversion inferred from exploration entropy not measured directly.
agent_relevance: A cognitive model and an LLM have complementary strengths; IBL is better with few observations. Hybrid with code-held memory is plausible.

source: Nguyen, Jamale, Gonzalez (2024) prompt design
finding: Prompts gave past trajectories as in-context demonstrations and asked for next path as coordinates with no explanation.
numbers: Max 31 steps per episode, -0.01 per move, -0.05 per obstacle; 206 and 194 humans in Exp1 and Exp2.
limits: No ablation of prompt content reported.
agent_relevance: Prediction of a person's next step from their past works from demonstrations alone. Useful if multiplayer users' data are read by agents.

source: Chen et al. (2025) DecisionFlow: LLM as principled decision maker
finding: A four-step prompt pipeline (extract actions and attributes, weight and filter, define utility, choose and justify) beats CoT on medical triage and agri/stock decisions.
numbers: GPT-4o MTA avg 79.25 vs 69.25 best baseline; DeLLMa avg 70.70 vs 60.00. Qwen2.5-14B Stocks 68.75 vs 28.33. GPT-4 MTA avg 66.50 vs 50.25.
limits: Not a win on Llama-3.1-8B (DeLLMa avg 72.36 vs 72.92; MTA high 76.17 vs 90.50). Eval sets 120-200 items, MTA partly GPT-4o generated.
agent_relevance: Structure that is not recognition-based (explicit utility) helps on option-choice tasks. Contrasts with RPD; shows the form of the decision matters.

source: Chen et al. (2025) DecisionFlow costs and failure modes
finding: Doing all four steps in one prompt did worse than separate calls. Early extraction and scoring errors propagate; scoring and filtering was the weakest step.
numbers: Prompt tokens about 7,900 vs 1,700 for CoT on DeLLMa; MTA latency about 28 s vs 2 s.
limits: Threshold epsilon tuned per dataset; prompting only.
agent_relevance: Supports one slot per call (program decides, model fills). Cost is about 4-14x; budget it.

source: Jalaeian, Morey, Rayo (2025) Joint activity design heuristics for human-machine collaboration
finding: Names five macrocognitive functions teams need (event detection, sensemaking, adaptability, perspective-shifting, coordination) and synthesizes 14 design heuristics for machines as team players.
numbers: 5 functions, 14 heuristics, 10 pages. Abstract only was read.
limits: No LLM experiment. Abstract does not describe how heuristics apply to LLMs.
agent_relevance: A checklist to audit our scaffold against the five functions. Gaps: perspective-shifting and event detection have no state yet.

source: Singh et al. (2025) LLMs in the SOC: empirical study of human-AI collaboration
finding: Real analysts used GPT-4 mainly as an explainer, not a decision maker: only about 4% of queries asked for a binary judgement like is this malicious.
numbers: 3,090 valid queries, 532 conversations, 45 analysts over 10 months. Command understanding 31% of tasks; 41% of conversations one-off; 34 low-use, 10 moderate, 1 power user (about 17% of queries).
limits: One SOC, one model, no accuracy or speed measures, novelty effect, disengagement reasons inferred.
agent_relevance: In the field, sensemaking support (explain, give context) is the use. Our agent may do best as sense-maker feeding a checked decision.

source: Singh et al. (2025) SOC engagement
finding: Thirteen analysts dropped off after 1-2 months, some after model errors or refusals; six stayed 4-8 months despite errors.
numbers: Active analysts rose from 4 (May 2023) to 25 (Feb 2024). Fleiss kappa of coding 0.75-0.90. 93% of queries mapped to a NICE element.
limits: Reasons for dropout not validated by interviews.
agent_relevance: Trust is lost on visible errors. Calibrated stated uncertainty and check results shown to the user matter for human-team use.

source: Edge et al. (2024) From local to global: GraphRAG for query-focused summarization
finding: Treats sensemaking over a whole corpus (global questions) as a summarization problem; a graph index with community summaries beats vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity.
numbers: 125 questions per dataset, 5 repeats. Podcast (about 1M tokens): comprehensiveness win 72-83%, diversity 75-82% vs vector RAG. News: 72-80% and 62-71%. Root-level C0: 72% and 62%.
limits: Two corpora around 1M tokens, GPT-4 judge, fabrication not measured, directness lost, empowerment mixed.
agent_relevance: A built-ahead structured frame (communities) helps sensemaking. Analogue to data-frame theory: pre-built frames, then fit data to them.

source: Edge et al. (2024) GraphRAG claim-based validation
finding: Claim counting confirmed the LLM judge: global methods yield more distinct claims than vector RAG.
numbers: 47,075 unique claims, average 31 per answer. Judge and claim labels agreed 78% (comprehensiveness) and 69-70% (diversity) on non-ties.
limits: Sensitive to tie threshold; claim extraction itself by LLM.
agent_relevance: Code-level counting of claims is a cheap check on judge verdicts (G5).

source: Gullstrand Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code review as decision-making
finding: A think-aloud study of 34 code reviews by 10 developers gave a two-phase model (orientation, then analysis) that resembles recognition-primed decision-making.
numbers: 10 developers, 34 reviews, 39 pages.
limits: No LLM experiment; model built bottom-up from small sample; abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Orient first, then analyse and plan, matches S-states of reading context before acting. Candidate order for a code-review mode.

source: Brown and Mulder (2025) LLMs as visualization agents for immersive binary reverse engineering
finding: An LLM agent with tool access to binary analysis was added to a VR environment whose affordances came from a cognitive systems engineering analysis. Pilot: usable 3D call graphs for small programs, but quality varies widely.
numbers: No participant counts or percentages reported in the abstract.
limits: Pilot, abstract only.
agent_relevance: CSE used to specify what the agent must support, then an LLM built on it. Shows the design-first order; output variance means a check step is needed.

source: Mastrianni et al. (2024) AI-enhanced sensemaking: generative AI assistant for genetic professionals
finding: Interviews and co-design found sensemaking is the main difficulty in whole-genome analysis and a process AI could support; gave three design considerations.
numbers: 17 interviewed, 6 co-designers. No quantitative results.
limits: Qualitative; no model sensemaking framework named; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Experts want help with sensemaking more than with the verdict. Matches c13.

source: Suh et al. (2026) Atlas: making sense of long-horizon agent trajectories
finding: A trajectory tree showing what an agent chose and set aside, with six artifact views, raised reported decision transparency and cut workload versus a baseline.
numbers: Within-subjects N=14, six representations. No effect sizes on the abstract page.
limits: Small N, subjective measures, stats not read.
agent_relevance: Sensemaking of the agent's own run by people. Our logs should expose rejected branches, not only final answers.

source: Storey (2026) Cognitive Tours: making understanding a deliverable in AI-assisted development
finding: Defines cognitive debt as eroded shared team understanding and intent debt as missing goals; proposes human-curated paths with AI audit.
numbers: None. 6-page demo paper, under review.
limits: No empirical validation.
agent_relevance: Warns that offloading sensemaking to agents erodes common ground. Keep a human-readable situation summary updated each run.

source: Sindelar and Bojar (2025) ELOQUENT 2025 Sensemaking task
finding: Teacher-student-evaluator test of text sensemaking. LLM judges wrongly accepted garbled and mixed-up question-answer pairs; students struggled to stay within the given text.
numbers: 7 sources, 4 languages, 4 teams, 6 systems submitted plus commercial baselines.
limits: Shared task overview; exact scores not read from the abstract.
agent_relevance: LLM graders are fooled by incoherent pairs. Supports G5: do not trust a model judge without an adversarial check.

source: Mainali et al. (2025) Classical AI vs LLMs for decision-maker alignment in health insurance choices
finding: A case-based classical system and LLM aligners (GPT-5, GPT-4 with weighted self-consistency) reach the same accuracy on matching a decision-maker's risk profile.
numbers: Overall accuracy: classical 0.892, GPT-5 0.895, GPT-4 0.892. 1,000 test probes. LLMs dropped on the moderate (0.5) target.
limits: No significance test; unequal inputs; only risk tolerance; NDM mentioned only in background.
agent_relevance: The LLM has no clear edge over a retrieval system on case-like decisions; case memory plus nearest neighbor is a strong baseline for RPD-style recognition.

source: Lim et al. (2025) TextBandit: probabilistic reasoning from text feedback
finding: Small LLMs mostly fail to learn the better arm from text feedback; only Qwen3-4B beat classical bandit baselines.
numbers: Two arms (30% vs 65%), 500 runs of 25 rounds. Best-arm rate Qwen3-4B 89.2%, Thompson 51.1%, UCB 47.6%, random 31.8%, Qwen3-8B 37.5%, Llama-3.1-8B 31.6%. Qwen3-4B fell to 6.53% with five arms.
limits: Small open models only, no human data, no CoT, overthinking claim untested.
agent_relevance: Learning an environment over many rounds is fragile in models and drops fast as options grow. Keep counts and posterior in code.

source: Huh and Mohapatra (2025) Grounding natural language for multi-agent decision-making with multi-agentic LLMs
finding: Ablates prompt engineering, memory, multimodal input and fine-tuning for multi-agent LLMs in social dilemma games.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; results not read.
agent_relevance: Coordination of several LLM agents is studied through games, not team macrocognition; no test of common ground found.

source: Search gap (this run) NDM and macrocognition in LLM agent loops
finding: An arXiv full-text search for macrocognition returned one paper (2512.08036). Search for recognition-primed returned one (2507.09637, code review). No paper found that implements pre-mortem, data-frame or RPD as an LLM loop with measured results besides the JMIR prompt study (c01).
numbers: Counts: macrocognition 1 result; recognition-primed 1; cognitive systems engineering plus language model 1 (2508.13413); sensemaking plus data-frame 314 mostly HCI.
limits: Search coverage limited: Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API were rate-limited, only 1 of 3 web searches ran, so gaps may be search artifacts.
agent_relevance: Little published evidence either way; our own tests of NDM operators would be new.
